The Assault of Gog, and God's Judgment on Him.</title> <div sID="gen21302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The objections to a literal interpretation of the prophecy are--</hi>(1) The ideal nature of the name Gog, which is the root of Magog, the only kindred name found in Scripture or history. (2) The nations congregated are selected from places most distant from Israel, and from one another, and therefore most unlikely to act in concert (Persians and Libyans, &c.). (3) The whole spoil of Israel could not have given a handful to a tithe of their number, or maintained the myriads of invaders a single day (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.12">Eze 38:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.13">13</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.4">4</reference>) The wood of their invaders' weapons was to serve for fuel to Israel for seven years! And all Israel were to take seven months in burying the dead! Supposing a million of Israelites to bury each two corpses a day, the aggregate buried in the hundred eighty working days of the seven months would be three hundred sixty millions of corpses! Then the pestilential vapors from such masses of victims before they were all buried! What Israelite could live in such an atmosphere? (5) The scene of the Lord's controversy here is different from that in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>, Edom, which creates a discrepancy. (But probably a different judgment is alluded to). (6) The gross carnality of the representation of God's dealings with His adversaries is inconsistent with Messianic times. It therefore requires a non-literal interpretation. The prophetical delineations of the divine principles of government are thrown into the familiar forms of Old Testament relations. The final triumph of Messiah's truth over the most distant and barbarous nations is represented as a literal conflict on a gigantic scale, Israel being the battlefield, ending in the complete triumph of Israel's anointed King, the Saviour of the world. It is a prophetical parable [Fairbairn]. However, though the details are not literal, the distinctiveness in this picture, characterizing also parallel descriptions in writers less ideally picturesque than Ezekiel, gives probability to a more definite and generally literal interpretation. The awful desolations caused in Judea by Antiochus Epiphanes, of Syria (1 Maccabees; and Porphyry, quoted by Jerome on Ezekiel), his defilement of Jehovah's temple by sacrificing swine and sprinkling the altar with the broth, and setting up the altar of Jupiter Olympius, seem to be an earnest of the final desolations to be caused by Antichrist in Israel, previous to His overthrow by the Lord Himself, coming to reign (compare Da 8:10-26; 11:21-45; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.3">3</reference>). Grotius explains Gog as a name taken from Gyges, king of Lydia; and Magog as Syria, in which was a city called Magog [Pliny, 5.28]. What Ezekiel stated more generally, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.9">Re 20:7-9</reference> states more definitely as to the anti-Christian confederacy which is to assail the beloved city.<div eID="gen21302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11765"/><hi type="bold">2. Gog--</hi>the prince of the land of Magog. The title was probably a common one of the kings of the country, as "Pharaoh" in Egypt. Chakan was the name given by the Northern Asiatics to their king, and is still a title of the Turkish sultan: "Gog" may be a contraction of this. In Ezekiel's time a horde of northern Asiatics, termed by the Greeks "Scythians," and probably including the Moschi and Tibareni, near the Caucasus, here ("Meshech ... Tubal") undertook an expedition against Egypt [Herodotus, 1.103-106]. These names might be adopted by Ezekiel from the historical fact familiar to men at the time, as ideal titles for the great last anti-Christian confederacy.<div eID="gen21303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Magog--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.10.2">Ge 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.5">1Ch 1:5</reference>). The name of a land belonging to Japheth's posterity. Maha, in Sanskrit, means "land." Gog is the ideal political head of the region. In <reference osisRef="Rev.20.8">Re 20:8</reference>, Gog and Magog are two peoples.<div eID="gen21304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the chief prince--</hi>rather, "prince of Rosh," or "Rhos" [Septuagint]. The Scythian Tauri in the Crimea were so called. The Araxes also was called "Rhos." The modern Russians may have hence assumed their name, as Moscow and Tobolsk from Meshech and Tubal, though their proper ancient name was Slavi, or Wends. Hengstenberg supports English Version, as "Rosh" is not found in the Bible. "Magog was Gog's original kingdom, though he acquired also Meshech and Tubal, so as to be called their chief prince." <div eID="gen21305" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 38 Eze 38:1-23 . The Assault of Gog, and God's Judgment on Him. (2) The nations congregated are selected from places most distant from Israel, and from one another, and therefore most unlikely to act in concert (Persians and Libyans, &c.). (3) The whole spoil of Israel could not have given a handful to a tithe of their number, or maintained the myriads of invaders a single day ( Eze 38:12 , 13 ). ( 4 ) The wood of their invaders' weapons was to serve for fuel to Israel for seven years! And all Israel were to take seven months in burying the dead! Supposing a million of Israelites to bury each two corpses a day, the aggregate buried in the hundred eighty working days of the seven months would be three hundred sixty millions of corpses! Then the pestilential vapors from such masses of victims before they were all buried! What Israelite could live in such an atmosphere? (5) The scene of the Lord's controversy here is different from that in Is 34:6 , Edom, which creates a discrepancy. (But probably a different judgment is alluded to). (6) The gross carnality of the representation of God's dealings with His adversaries is inconsistent with Messianic times. It therefore requires a non-literal interpretation. The prophetical delineations of the divine principles of government are thrown into the familiar forms of Old Testament relations. The final triumph of Messiah's truth over the most distant and barbarous nations is represented as a literal conflict on a gigantic scale, Israel being the battlefield, ending in the complete triumph of Israel's anointed King, the Saviour of the world. It is a prophetical parable [Fairbairn]. What Ezekiel stated more generally, Re 20:7-9 states more definitely as to the anti-Christian confederacy which is to assail the beloved city. 2. Gog-- the prince of the land of Magog. Tubal") undertook an expedition against Egypt [Herodotus, 1.103-106]. These names might be adopted by Ezekiel from the historical fact familiar to men at the time, as ideal titles for the great last anti-Christian confederacy. Magog-- ( Ge 10:2 ; 1Ch 1:5 ). The name of a land belonging to Japheth's posterity. Maha, in Sanskrit, means "land." Gog is the ideal political head of the region. In Re 20:8 , Gog and Magog are two peoples. the chief prince-- rather, "prince of Rosh," or "Rhos" [Septuagint]. The Scythian Tauri in the Crimea were so called. The Araxes also was called "Rhos." The modern Russians may have hence assumed their name, as Moscow and Tobolsk from Meshech and Tubal, though their proper ancient name was Slavi, or Wends. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11771"/><div sID="gen21314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11771"/><hi type="bold">8. thou shall be visited--</hi>in wrath, by God (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>). Probably there is allusion to <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Is 24:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.22">22</reference>, "The host of the high ones ... shall be gathered ... as prisoners ... in the pit ... and after many days shall they be visited." I therefore prefer English Version to Grotius rendering, "Thou shalt get the command" of the expedition. The "after many days" is defined by "in the latter years," that is, in the times just before the coming of Messiah, namely, under Antiochus, before His first coming; under Antichrist, before His second coming.<div eID="gen21314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mountains of Israel ... always waste--</hi>that is, waste during the long period of the captivity, the earnest of the much longer period of Judea's present desolation (to which the language "always waste" more fully applies). This marks the impious atrocity of the act, to assail God's people, who had only begun to recover from their protracted calamities.<div eID="gen21315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but it is brought ... and they shall dwell--</hi>rather, "And they (the Israelites) were brought ... dwelt safely" [Fairbairn]. English Version means, "Against Israel, which has been waste, but which (that is, whose people) is now (at the time of the invasion) brought forth out of the nations where they were dispersed, and shall be found by the invader dwelling securely, so as to seem an easy prey to him." <div eID="gen21316" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 8. thou shall be visited-- in wrath, by God ( Is 29:6 ). Probably there is allusion to Is 24:21 , 22 , "The host of the high ones ... shall be gathered ... as prisoners ... in the pit ... and after many days shall they be visited." I therefore prefer English Version to Grotius rendering, "Thou shalt get the command" of the expedition. The "after many days" is defined by "in the latter years," that is, in the times just before the coming of Messiah, namely, under Antiochus, before His first coming; under Antichrist, before His second coming. the mountains of Israel ... always waste-- that is, waste during the long period of the captivity, the earnest of the much longer period of Judea's present desolation (to which the language "always waste" more fully applies). So, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.5">Eze 5:5</reference>, Israel is said to be set "in the midst of the nations"; not physically, but morally, a central position for being a blessing to the world: so (as the favored or "beloved city," <reference osisRef="Rev.20.9">Re 20:9</reference>) an object of envy. Grotius translates, "In the height of the land" (so <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.8">Eze 38:8</reference>), "the mountains of Israel," Israel being morally elevated above the rest of the world. <div eID="gen21320" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11779"/><div sID="gen21325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11779"/><hi type="bold">17. thou he of whom I have spoken in old time--</hi>Gog, &c. are here identified with the enemies spoken of in other prophecies (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17-Num.24.24">Nu 24:17-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.23">Jr 30:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.1">Joe 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.6">6</reference>; Is 14:12-14; 59:<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">19</reference>). God is represented as addressing Gog at the time of his assault; therefore, the "old time" is the time long prior, when Ezekiel uttered these prophecies; so, he also, as well as Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45">Da 11:1-45</reference>) and Zechariah (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.21">Zec 14:1-21</reference>) are included among "the prophets of Israel" here.<div eID="gen21325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many years--</hi>ago. <div eID="gen21326" type="x-p"/>

God is represented as addressing Gog at the time of his assault; therefore, the "old time" is the time long prior, when Ezekiel uttered these prophecies; so, he also, as well as Daniel ( Da 11:1-45 ) and Zechariah ( Zec 14:1-21 ) are included among "the prophets of Israel" here. many years-- ago.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11782"/><div sID="gen21329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11782"/><hi type="bold">20. fishes--</hi>disturbed by the fleets which I will bring.<div eID="gen21329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fowls, &c.--</hi>frightened at the sight of so many men: an ideal picture.<div eID="gen21330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountains--</hi>that is, the fortresses on the mountains.<div eID="gen21331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steep places--</hi>literally, "stairs" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">So 2:14</reference>); steep terraces for vines on the sides of hills, to prevent the earth being washed down by the rains.<div eID="gen21332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every wall--</hi>of towns. <div eID="gen21333" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 20. fishes-- disturbed by the fleets which I will bring. fowls, &c.-- frightened at the sight of so many men: an ideal picture. mountains-- that is, the fortresses on the mountains. steep places-- literally, "stairs" ( So 2:14 ); steep terraces for vines on the sides of hills, to prevent the earth being washed down by the rains. every wall-- of towns.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11784"/><div sID="gen21335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11784"/><hi type="bold">22. plead--</hi>a forensic term; because God in His inflictions acts on the principles of His own immutable justice, not by arbitrary impulse (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.16">Is 66:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">Jr 25:31</reference>).<div eID="gen21335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood ... hailstones, fire--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.8.7">Re 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.21">16:21</reference>). The imagery is taken from the destruction of Sodom and the plagues of Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>). Antiochus died by "pestilence" (2 Maccabees 9:5). <chapter eID="Ezek.38"/>
